# === Core ===

# sequence. The value must be unique: the schema queries every other project and refuses a
# duplicate, so 1 is a starting guess rather than a decision, and only you can see what the

image: portfolio-cover.jpg
# docs/images/portfolio-cover.jpg, 2000x1125. Set the hotspot on the violet bar, which is
# the row a reader should land on when the hero crops.

description: >-
  A fine-tuned sentence-transformer that scores how well a resume fits a job posting on a
  calibrated 0 to 1 scale, explains which requirements are missing, and is measured only on
  postings it has never seen.

longDescription: >-
  ResumeAI scores resume and job-posting fit, and is really a study of how to find out
  whether a score means anything.

  The model is a bi-encoder: MPNet embeddings fine-tuned on 815 curated pairs built from 255
  real job postings, then Platt-calibrated so the number can be read as a percentage rather
  than a cosine similarity. On 106 pairs from 53 postings that never appear in training, it
  reaches 0.827 Spearman and picks the strongest of four candidates first for 84.9% of
  postings, ahead of a frontier LLM scoring the same pairs zero-shot.

  The modelling took an afternoon. The rest of the project is the part that transfers: an
  external test set that caught the best internal model inverting on unseen data, a paired
  cluster bootstrap behind every comparison, a multiplicity correction that reduced ten
  significant results to one, a pre-registered ablation that removed half the production
  loss function, and a set of causal interventions that found the shipped model rewards
  keyword stuffing, which 0.82 Spearman had concealed completely.

# === 1. Problem, goal, outcome ===
# Three parallel cards. Kept to similar lengths so none of them stretches the row.

problem: >-
  Keyword screening scores a QA engineer who writes Python test scripts highly against a
  Python backend posting: same words, wrong role. Embedding models fix the ordering and
  introduce a different failure, because any two English documents share a similarity floor,
  so every score lands between 0.5 and 0.9 and a 16% match is displayed as 78%. Both
  failures are invisible to the metric usually reported, since a model can rank well while
  its numbers mean nothing, and can score well on a test split drawn from postings it
  trained on.

goal: >-
  Build a matcher that ranks candidates correctly on postings it has never seen, produces
  absolute scores a user can read as a percentage, explains every verdict at the level of
  individual requirements, and, for each of those three claims, produces evidence that
  survives resampling rather than a single point estimate. Success was defined before the
  runs: beat the non-neural baselines and the off-the-shelf model on external data, with the
  difference tested rather than asserted.

outcome: >-
  On 106 pairs from unseen postings the model reaches 0.827 +/- 0.024 Spearman and 0.119
  +/- 0.011 MAE across three seeds, and picks the best of four candidates first for 84.9% of
  53 postings against a 25% random baseline. A paired cluster bootstrap separates it from
  base MPNet, TF-IDF, word overlap, and Claude Opus 4.5. The study is equally a record of
  what failed: a rejected cross-encoder, four fixes that did not work, an ablation that
  removed a shipped design choice, and three of four behavioural tests the model fails.

# === 2. Dataset and model ===
# Spec rows, not paragraphs. Source: docs/DATA_CARD.md and Results/results_summary.json.

datasetSource: >-
  ~1,150 scraped LinkedIn postings, curated to 255 unique training postings plus 53 held
  out, across 14 industries and 4 seniority levels. Resume text and match scores are
  synthetically generated against those real postings and hand-curated.
datasetSize: "1,027 labelled pairs: 815 training from 255 postings, 212 external from 53 postings with zero overlap, split 106 calibration and 106 final test"
datasetClasses: "5 match types: strong, good, partial, hard negative, weak"
datasetPreprocessing: >-
  Requirement-first JD truncation that strips EEO, benefits and salary boilerplate at a
  350-word cut; 3x augmentation by section shuffling, sentence dropping, keyword noise and
  +/-0.02 score jitter; splits stratified by match type at seed 42, with the zero
  training-to-external posting overlap asserted in code rather than assumed.

modelUsed: "Fine-tuned all-mpnet-base-v2 bi-encoder, 109M parameters, plus a 2-parameter Platt calibrator"
modelApproach: >-
  Chosen against a RoBERTa cross-encoder that scored higher internally and inverted on
  unseen postings. Trained with CoSENT for ranking plus CosineSimilarity for absolute score,
  then calibrated post-hoc on a separate external split so the score mapping generalises.
  Platt ships over isotonic on a robustness argument rather than a metric win, since the two
  are statistically tied and a 2-parameter sigmoid cannot overfit a 106-pair split. A later
  pre-registered ablation found the CosineSimilarity half contributes nothing measurable
  once calibration is applied.
modelTraining: "4 epochs, batch 16, 10% warmup, AMP mixed precision, seeds 42/43/44, about 24 minutes per seed on a Colab T4"
modelEvaluation: >-
  Spearman for ranking and MAE for calibration on a 106-pair external final test, reported
  as a mean across three seeds with cluster-bootstrap intervals that resample postings
  rather than pairs. Every baseline is scored on the identical pairs: word overlap, TF-IDF,
  base MPNet, and Claude Opus 4.5 under the same calibration protocol. Plus precision@1 over
  53 postings, a reliability diagram, a name-substitution bias audit, and four behavioural
  interventions. Internal-only evaluation was rejected after it inflated a cross-encoder by
  1.5 Spearman points.

# === 3. Pipeline ===
# Verb-first and short; the rail auto-picks an icon from keywords and clamps labels at about
# 14 characters before wrapping.
pipelineSteps:
  - "Ingest resume & JD"
  - "Clean & truncate"
  - "Augment pairs"
  - "Train bi-encoder"
  - "Calibrate score"
  - "Evaluate unseen JDs"

# === 4. Results ===
# Numeric entries become the count-up slider; entries with textValue become Highlights.
# Sources: Results/results_summary.json, Results/significance.json, Results/behavioral_tests.json.
resultsMetrics:
  - label: "Precision@1, unseen postings"
    value: 84.9
    unit: "%"
    description: >-
      The model ranks the strongest of four candidates first for 45 of 53 postings it never
      trained on, against 25% from guessing. Wilson 95% interval [73%, 92%], exact binomial
      p = 7.6e-20. Ranking is invariant to calibration, so this uses raw scores.
  - label: "Spearman, held-out postings"
    value: 0.8273
    description: >-
      Mean across seeds 42, 43 and 44, standard deviation 0.0236, on 106 pairs from 53
      postings with zero overlap with training. The published production seed scores
      0.8163, and the checkpoint on the Hub was re-downloaded and confirmed to reproduce it.
  - label: "Mean absolute error"
    value: 0.1194
    description: >-
      After Platt calibration, down from 0.1605 raw. Calibration is strictly increasing, so
      it cannot change the ranking: Spearman is identical before and after, and only the
      readability of the number changed.
  - label: "Spearman gained over Claude Opus 4.5"
    value: 0.105
    description: >-
      Frontier LLM, zero-shot, scoring the identical 106 pairs through the same calibration
      protocol. Paired cluster bootstrap over postings, 95% CI [+0.020, +0.212], p = 0.012
      after Holm correction. A matched floor rather than Claude's ceiling: the fine-tuned
      model saw 815 in-domain labelled pairs and Claude saw none.
  - label: "Behavioural tests passed"
    textValue: "1 of 4"
    description: >-
      Four interventions, each changing one thing about a held-out resume, with the expected
      direction written down first. The score falls when the evidence it cited is removed,
      which is the result the product depends on. It also rises for unevidenced keywords on
      52 of 52 resumes, rises for empty filler, and moves when sentences are reordered
      without changing a word. Reported in full rather than filtered.
  - label: "Comparisons surviving correction"
    textValue: "1 of 3"
    description: >-
      The loss ablation reported ten bootstrap comparisons and called three significant.
      Corrected for the size of the family they belong to, one survives.
  - label: "Training postings the model saw"
    textValue: "Zero of the 53 tested"
    description: >-
      Overlap between the training postings and the external set is asserted in code, not
      assumed, and the assertion runs in the test suite.

resultImages:
  - title: "Every engine on the same 106 held-out pairs"
    image: fig-engine-ladder.png
    caption: >-
      Notice what the baselines already achieve. Word overlap reaches 0.559 and TF-IDF 0.566,
      so a study reporting only the fine-tuned 0.816 would be hiding most of its own context.
      Whiskers are 95% intervals from a bootstrap that resamples postings rather than pairs,
      because four candidates from one posting are not four independent observations.
  - title: "Four interventions, one pass"
    image: fig-behavioral-tests.png
    caption: >-
      The result correlational evaluation could not produce. Removing the sentence the model
      cited as evidence costs 0.045, which is the behaviour the product claims. Adding
      unevidenced tool names raises the score on all 52 resumes tested, reordering sentences
      moves it by a third of the model's typical error, and empty filler is rewarded. Three
      real weaknesses that 0.82 Spearman concealed.
  - title: "What calibration changed, and what it did not"
    image: fig-calibration.png
    caption: >-
      Before calibration the bottom third of the scale is unreachable, so a weak match is
      displayed as 0.4. Platt scaling is strictly increasing, so it recovers the range and
      cuts mean absolute error from 0.180 to 0.127 while leaving Spearman at 0.8164 exactly.
      The top of the scale stays out of reach either way, which is why the output is
      documented as a ranking signal rather than a percentage fit.
  - title: "The cross-encoder inversion"
    image: 03_external_validation_fig1.png
    caption: >-
      The finding that redirected the project. A RoBERTa cross-encoder won the internal test
      at 0.8917 Spearman and scored -0.6122 on postings outside the training pool, ranking
      good candidates below bad ones. At 125M parameters over 400 examples it had memorised
      the training postings. The calibrated bi-encoder lost 0.076 across the same transfer.
  - title: "Four fixes, none of them enough"
    image: 04_overfitting_fixes_fig1.png
    caption: >-
      Augmentation, weight decay, a smaller backbone and a 5-fold ensemble, ablated one at a
      time. Every fix helped, moving external Spearman from -0.35 to +0.51, and none beat the
      simpler calibrated bi-encoder at 0.77. At this data scale, cross-encoder capacity is a
      liability rather than an advantage.
  - title: "Name-substitution bias audit"
    image: model_audit.png
    caption: >-
      18 name pairs across 6 demographic groups substituted into all 106 test resumes with
      everything else held constant. The largest group gap is 0.0054, statistically
      detectable and about a twentieth of the model's own mean absolute error, and 3 of 106
      pairs cross a verdict band on the name alone. It tests names only, and says nothing
      about school, address or employment gaps.
  - title: "The held-out benchmark, pair by pair"
    image: demo-benchmark.jpg
    caption: >-
      A demo page for reading the evidence rather than the summary. Filter the 106 held-out
      pairs by match type or industry, compare every engine on the same pair, and read the
      resume and posting behind each score.

# === 6. Challenges and insights ===
# `challenge` is one line; `solution` is one to three sentences.
challengesSolutions:
  - challenge: "The best internal model, a cross-encoder at 0.8917 Spearman, scored -0.6122 on postings outside the training pool."
    solution: >-
      Built a 212-pair external test from 53 unseen postings with zero overlap asserted in
      code, made it the only reported metric, and ablated four fixes against it. Every fix
      helped and none beat the simpler calibrated bi-encoder, so the evidence rather than
      the leaderboard picked the architecture that shipped.
  - challenge: "0.82 Spearman said the score was right, and said nothing about what the score was reading."
    solution: >-
      Ran four interventions on held-out resumes with the expected direction fixed in
      advance. One passed. The model rewards unevidenced keywords on 52 of 52 resumes, which
      contradicted a warning the product was showing users, so the copy was corrected and a
      test now fails if any user-facing string claims the model catches stuffing.
  - challenge: "CoSENT-trained bi-encoders compress every score into roughly 0.5 to 0.9, so a 16% match displays as 78%."
    solution: >-
      Fitted a post-hoc calibrator on a held-out external split, cutting MAE from 0.180 to
      0.127 while leaving the ranking untouched, since a strictly increasing map cannot
      change ranks. The residual compression is quantified rather than hidden: strong
      matches are still underscored by 0.166, so the output is documented as a ranking
      signal.
  - challenge: "Two production runs published a model that did not match its published metrics."
    solution: >-
      SentenceTransformer.fit() defaults to save_best_model=True, so the saved directory held
      the best-by-validation checkpoint while the calibrator was fitted to the final epoch
      still in memory. Nothing raised an error. The pipeline now reloads the saved checkpoint
      before calibrating, and three guards fail loudly: the training run re-downloads and
      verifies its own publication, the audit aborts on a mismatch above 0.01 Spearman, and
      the demo build refuses to bundle predictions that fail the same check.
  - challenge: "The one design choice that was reasoning rather than evidence was the loss function that actually shipped."
    solution: >-
      Pre-registered a three-arm, three-seed ablation with the hypothesis and predicted
      mechanism committed before any run, matching gradient-step counts across arms so the
      loss could not be confounded with a longer schedule. After calibration, CoSENT alone
      is indistinguishable from the combined objective. Then the same scrutiny went to that
      result: corrected for its family, one of three significant comparisons survives, and an
      equivalence test shows the null is a failure to detect rather than a demonstrated tie.

keyInsights:
  - title: "External validation is not optional"
    description: >-
      A held-out split drawn from the same posting pool still flattered the cross-encoder by
      1.5 Spearman points. The only split that told the truth was one where no posting
      appeared on both sides.
  - title: "Correlation hides what a model reads"
    description: >-
      A model reading style instead of skills produces the same 0.82. Four interventions,
      built in an afternoon and needing no labels, found three weaknesses that every
      correlational metric in the project had missed.
  - title: "Measure the artifact you ship"
    description: >-
      A default argument silently decoupled the published model from the published metrics.
      The fix was not vigilance, it was three guards that compare the artifact against its
      own reported numbers and fail loudly.
  - title: "Count the comparisons first"
    description: >-
      Ten bootstrap tests produced three results under p = 0.05. Corrected within the family
      they belong to, one survives. And a null is not a finding until you state what the
      test could have detected.
  - title: "The labels bound the question"
    description: >-
      Synthetic labels answer whether a model can learn this rubric. They cannot answer
      whether it predicts job fit, and no amount of statistical care closes that gap, because
      the gap is in the data rather than the analysis.

# === 7. Impact tiles ===
# Deliberately not model metrics, which live in resultsMetrics above.
impact:
  - label: "Held-out postings"
    textValue: "53, zero overlap"
    description: "Asserted in code and re-checked by the test suite, not assumed from how the split was built."
  - label: "Every difference resampled"
    textValue: "10,000 draws"
    description: "Paired cluster bootstrap at the posting level, with Holm correction inside each family of comparisons."
  - label: "Test suite"
    textValue: "222 tests, fully offline"
    description: "No model downloads, no API calls. Runs on every push, alongside a linter."
  - label: "Serving footprint"
    textValue: "109M parameters, CPU"
    description: "The model that beat a frontier LLM on this task fits on a free-tier container."

# === 8. Learnings and next steps ===
whatILearned: >-
  This project taught me that evaluation design decides more than model choice. I started by
  chasing the architecture with the best internal number and shipped the weaker one, because
  it was the only one that survived contact with unseen data.

  The harder lesson came later. The parts of a system least likely to be examined are the
  parts that already appear to work. I had ablated four cross-encoder fixes that failed
  while the loss function actually running in production rested on an argument I had never
  tested; when I finally pre-registered a test for it, the argument did not hold and half
  the objective came out. The same thing happened again with the score itself. It correlated
  well, so I never asked what it was responding to, and the first four interventions I wrote
  found that it rewards keyword stuffing on every resume tested. That result contradicted a
  warning the product was showing to users, which made it a correction to ship rather than a
  paragraph to write.

  The last lesson was about where the ceiling actually is. After multiplicity correction,
  equivalence testing and power analysis, the binding constraint turned out to be neither
  the model nor the analysis but the labels: they are synthetic, so the study answers whether
  a model can learn this rubric and cannot answer whether it predicts job fit. Recognising
  that a limitation lives in the evidence rather than the method, and then costing the
  experiment that would remove it instead of writing a caveat about it, is the part of this
  project I would carry into any other one.

nextSteps:
  - "Tier 1, the unlock: about 300 blinded pairwise expert comparisons over the 53 held-out postings, reporting the inter-rater agreement ceiling as the headline. Real labels are needed for validation rather than training, which puts this at a weekend and a few hundred dollars"
  - "Tier 2: score real resumes against the same postings, to test whether the numbers survive contact with formatting debris, abbreviations and gaps"
  - "Tier 3: score-to-outcome data through the product, with range restriction, ghosting as its own category, and explicit opt-in"
  - "Efficiency study, designed and scaffolded but not yet run. Five ways of serving the same model, measured on the same 106 pairs: PyTorch fp32 as the reference, int8 dynamic quantisation, ONNX Runtime in fp32 and int8, and the 3-seed ensemble. The decision rule is fixed before the first run, so an arm counts as adoptable only when its Spearman sits inside the project's own 0.0174 reproducibility margin of fp32 and its p95 latency is lower"
  - "That study exists because two claims in this repository are currently adjectives rather than numbers. The shipped service loads 420 MB of weights onto a scale-to-zero CPU container and cold-starts in 30 to 60 seconds, none of which has been measured, and the 3-seed ensemble reached 0.8639 against the shipped 0.8163 but was rejected for tripling serving cost, a cost nobody costed. Design in docs/EFFICIENCY_STUDY.md, harness in scripts/benchmark_inference.py, results to Results/inference_benchmark.json"
  - "Retrain against the keyword-stuffing failure, whose hard negatives were wrong-role resumes rather than plausible resumes with a skills line bolted on"
  - "Posting-grouped calibration split, implemented behind a flag and awaiting a re-run"
  - "Full plan and costings in docs/VALIDATION_ROADMAP.md"

    description: >-
      Measured on the reliability diagram over the held-out pairs. Low, with one caveat
      stated rather than buried: predictions stop at 0.852 while the labels reach 0.945, so
      the model never uses the top of its own scale.
  - label: "Mean absolute error, before and after"
    textValue: "0.180 down to 0.127"
    description: >-
      What post-hoc Platt calibration bought. The ranking is untouched, because a strictly
      increasing map cannot reorder anything, so only the readability of the number changed.
  - label: "Demographic name-substitution spread"
    value: 0.0054
    description: >-
      18 name pairs across 6 groups substituted into all 106 test resumes with every skill,
      date and employer held constant. Statistically detectable and about a twentieth of the
      model's own mean absolute error. 3 of 106 pairs cross a verdict band on the name alone.
  - label: "Scoring methods on the identical pairs"
    value: 5
    description: >-
      Word overlap, TF-IDF, base MPNet, Claude Opus 4.5 and the fine-tuned model, each scored
      on the same 106 pairs so the comparison is like for like rather than like for anecdote.

---

ResumeAI scores how well a resume fits a job posting, and is really a study of how to find
out whether a score means anything.

The model is ordinary on purpose. Fine-tuned MPNet embeddings, Platt-calibrated, 109M
parameters, trained in about 24 minutes on a free Colab GPU. Anyone can build it. The effort
went into the evaluation, because that is the part that transfers to a different problem.

On 106 pairs from 53 postings that never appear in training, it reaches **0.827 Spearman**
and ranks the strongest of four candidates first for **84.9% of postings** where guessing
gets 25%. It **outranks Claude Opus 4.5** on the identical pairs by 0.105 Spearman (95% CI
[+0.020, +0.212], p = 0.012). Every baseline is scored on the same pairs, which matters,
because word overlap alone reaches 0.559 and a study that reported only its own headline
would be hiding most of its context.

Four findings say more about the work than the headline does.

**The best internal model was the worst real one.** A RoBERTa cross-encoder scored 0.8917 on
an internal split and -0.6122 on postings outside the training pool, ranking good candidates
below bad ones. It had memorised 150 postings. Four anti-overfitting fixes were ablated
against a proper external set; every one helped, none beat the simpler calibrated bi-encoder,
and the evidence rather than the leaderboard picked what shipped.

**The release process had a defect that no metric would ever show.**
`SentenceTransformer.fit()` saves the best-by-validation checkpoint while leaving the final
epoch in memory, so an early production run published a model whose calibrator had been
fitted to different weights. An automated cross-check between the training run and the audit
found it, and three guards now make that class of failure impossible to miss.

**The statistics were turned on the study's own conclusions.** A pre-registered ablation
could not distinguish the shipped loss function from half of it. That ablation reported ten
bootstrap comparisons and called three significant; corrected for the family they belong to,
one survives. The central null turned out to be a limit rather than a finding, since the
comparison can detect 0.045 Spearman and would need to rule out 0.017, so it was never able
to answer its own question. Settling it needs roughly 338 postings against the 50 available.

**Correlation never said what the model was reading.** Four interventions, each changing one
thing about a held-out resume with the direction written down first, found that removing the
sentence the model cited as evidence costs 0.045, and that everything else fails: unevidenced
keywords raise the score on 52 of 52 resumes, empty senior-sounding filler is rewarded, and
reordering sentences without changing a word moves the score by a third of its typical error.
The keyword result contradicted a warning the product was showing to users, so the copy was
corrected and a test now fails if any user-facing string claims the model detects stuffing.

The honest summary is that this project measures how faithfully a model reproduces a scoring
rubric the project wrote, on postings it has never seen. It does not measure whether the
model predicts job fit, because the labels are synthetic and no amount of methodological care
closes that gap. `docs/VALIDATION_ROADMAP.md` costs the experiment that would: roughly 300
blinded pairwise comparisons from real recruiters, reporting the human agreement ceiling as
the headline rather than the model.
